title: The four tissue types
blurb: Identify epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous tissue from their features, name epithelia by layer and shape, and tell exocrine from endocrine glands.
question: A student scrapes off the top layer of skin on her knee. The scrape stings and weeps a little but does not bleed. What type of tissue was removed, and what feature of that tissue explains the lack of bleeding?

teach.body: A tissue is a group of similar cells working together on a shared function. The body has only four primary types: epithelial tissue covers and lines, connective tissue supports and binds, muscle tissue contracts, and nervous tissue conducts impulses. Plain English: covering, support, movement and control. Every organ is some mix of these four.

teach.h: The four tissue types at a glance
teach.caption: Connective tissue is the most abundant and widespread of the four.

teach.body: Epithelium covers body surfaces, lines cavities and tubes, and forms glands. Its cells are tightly packed and sit on a basement membrane, with an apical (free) surface and a basal surface: this is called polarity. Epithelium is avascular: it has no blood vessels and is fed by diffusion from the connective tissue beneath. It regenerates quickly, which suits a tissue that is constantly worn away.

teach.caption: Combine the two parts: the epidermis is stratified squamous epithelium (many layers, flat cells on top).

teach.h: Connective tissue: support in a matrix
teach.body: Connective tissue is the most abundant tissue. Its cells are scattered in an extracellular matrix of ground substance plus fibers (collagen, elastic and reticular). It is usually vascular, but cartilage is avascular. Examples: bone, cartilage, adipose (fat), areolar tissue, dense regular tissue in tendons and ligaments, and blood, whose matrix is the fluid plasma.

teach.caption: All muscle tissue is contractile and excitable. Smooth muscle also sits in the walls of blood vessels and airways.

teach.body: Nervous tissue has two cell groups: neurons, which conduct impulses, and neuroglia, which support and protect them. Glands are made of epithelium. Exocrine glands secrete through ducts onto a surface (sweat, salivary, pancreatic enzymes). Endocrine glands are ductless and release hormones into the blood. The pancreas is both: it sends enzymes down a duct and hormones into the blood.

teach.caption: The pancreas belongs in both columns: digestive enzymes (exocrine) and insulin and glucagon (endocrine).

teach.body: Marisol, a nursing applicant, scrapes her knee on a sidewalk. Only the epidermis comes off, so the wound weeps but does not bleed. The epidermis is stratified squamous epithelium, and epithelium is avascular. Had the scrape reached the dermis beneath, which is vascular connective tissue, it would have bled. Within days the fast-regenerating epithelium covers the area again.

teach.text: Exam favorites: epithelium HAS no blood vessels (it is avascular), and cartilage is the connective tissue that is also avascular. Blood is a connective tissue, not its own tissue type. Pseudostratified epithelium only LOOKS layered: it is a single layer.

items: Four types: epithelial (cover), connective (support), muscle (contract), nervous (conduct).
Epithelium: tightly packed, basement membrane, avascular, regenerates fast.
Name epithelia by layers (simple, stratified) and shape (squamous, cuboidal, columnar).
Connective tissue: cells in a matrix; most abundant; cartilage is avascular; blood counts.
Exocrine glands use ducts; endocrine glands release hormones into blood; pancreas does both.

summary: You can now name the four tissue types and recognize each from its features, including avascular epithelium and matrix-filled connective tissue. You can also decode epithelial names and classify glands as exocrine or endocrine.

A.q: Which tissue is avascular and is nourished by diffusion from the tissue beneath it?
A.why: Epithelium has no blood vessels; nutrients diffuse up from the vascular connective tissue under its basement membrane.

whyNot.1: Areolar tissue is a vascular connective tissue; it is the source the epithelium relies on, not the avascular layer.
whyNot.2: Smooth muscle has its own blood supply.
whyNot.3: Nervous tissue is well supplied with blood vessels.

A.q: Which feature is characteristic of connective tissue?
options: Cells tightly packed with little space between
Cells scattered within an extracellular matrix
Cells that are excitable and able to contract
Cells with an apical and a basal surface
A.why: Connective tissue cells are spread out in a matrix of ground substance and fibers (collagen, elastic, reticular).

whyNot.0: Tightly packed cells describe epithelial tissue.
whyNot.2: Excitable, contractile cells describe muscle tissue.
whyNot.3: An apical and a basal surface (polarity) is a feature of epithelial tissue.

A.q: An epithelium looks layered under the microscope, yet every one of its cells rests on the basement membrane. What is it called?
A.why: Pseudostratified epithelium appears layered but is a single layer, because every cell touches the basement membrane.

whyNot.0: Stratified epithelium truly has two or more layers, so not every cell reaches the basement membrane.
whyNot.1: Transitional epithelium is a stretchy, truly layered epithelium found in the bladder.
whyNot.3: Simple cuboidal is one layer of cube-shaped cells and does not look layered.

B.q: Which tissue lines the urinary bladder and allows it to stretch as it fills?
B.why: Transitional epithelium changes shape as it stretches, which suits the bladder.

whyNot.0: Simple squamous epithelium is a single thin layer suited to diffusion, not to stretching.
whyNot.1: Dense regular connective tissue forms tendons and ligaments, not organ linings.
whyNot.2: Stratified cuboidal epithelium does not have the stretch of transitional epithelium.

B.q: Tendons and ligaments are made mainly of which tissue?
B.why: Tendons and ligaments are dense regular connective tissue: tightly packed parallel collagen fibers for strength.

whyNot.1: Areolar tissue is loose connective tissue, not the dense fibers that make tendons and ligaments.
whyNot.2: Tendons attach muscle to bone, but they are not made of muscle tissue.
whyNot.3: Stratified squamous epithelium covers surfaces such as the epidermis.

B.q: Which gland functions as BOTH an exocrine and an endocrine gland?
B.why: The pancreas secretes digestive enzymes through a duct (exocrine) and hormones such as insulin into the blood (endocrine).

whyNot.0: Salivary glands secrete saliva through ducts: exocrine only.
whyNot.1: Sweat glands secrete sweat through ducts onto the skin: exocrine only.
whyNot.3: The thyroid releases hormones into the blood without ducts: endocrine only.

C.q: Tomas scrapes off the outermost layer of skin on his elbow. The wound stings but does not bleed. Which statement BEST explains this?
options: The epidermis is connective tissue with no vessels
The epidermis is epithelial tissue with no vessels
The dermis is epithelial tissue with no vessels
The epidermis is vascular, but its vessels constrict
C.why: The epidermis is stratified squamous epithelium, and epithelium is avascular, so removing it alone causes no bleeding.

whyNot.0: The epidermis is epithelial, not connective tissue.
whyNot.2: The dermis is vascular connective tissue; it would bleed if reached, and it is not the outermost layer.
whyNot.3: The epidermis has no blood vessels at all, so there are none to constrict.

C.q: Which statement about tissue types is CORRECT?
options: Cartilage has a rich blood supply, so it heals fast
Neuroglia are the cells that conduct nerve impulses
Smooth muscle is striated and under voluntary control
Blood is a connective tissue with a fluid matrix
C.why: Blood is classed as connective tissue: its cells are suspended in plasma, a fluid extracellular matrix.

whyNot.0: Cartilage is avascular, which is why it heals slowly.
whyNot.1: Neurons conduct impulses; neuroglia support and protect the neurons.
whyNot.2: Smooth muscle is non-striated and involuntary.

C.q: A slide shows branched, striated cells with one nucleus each, joined end to end by intercalated discs. Which tissue is this?
C.why: Branched striated cells joined by intercalated discs are cardiac muscle, found only in the heart wall.

whyNot.0: Skeletal muscle is striated but its fibers are long, cylindrical and multinucleated, with no intercalated discs.
whyNot.1: Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped and not striated.
whyNot.2: Dense regular connective tissue is parallel collagen fibers with scattered cells, not contractile cells.

reteach.title: Think of the body as a house
reteach.question: A house needs paint and tiles, a frame and pipes, motors, and electrical wiring. Which tissue type plays each role in the body?

blocks.body: Epithelium is the paint, siding and tiles: it covers every surface and lines every pipe, and it has no plumbing of its own. Connective tissue is the frame, beams and the water in the pipes: bone holds things up, tendons tie things together, and blood moves supplies. Muscle is the motors that move the doors. Nervous tissue is the wiring that switches everything on.

blocks.text: Paint has no pipes of its own: epithelium is avascular and is fed by the connective tissue underneath it.

explain.body: Covers and lines; tightly packed cells on a basement membrane; avascular. Named by layers (simple, stratified) plus shape (squamous, cuboidal, columnar).

test.q: Stratified squamous epithelium is made of
test.why: Stratified means two or more layers; squamous means flat.

whyNot.0: One layer of flat cells is simple squamous epithelium.
whyNot.2: One layer of tall cells is simple columnar epithelium.
whyNot.3: Cube-shaped cells are cuboidal, not squamous.

explain.body: Cells scattered in a matrix of ground substance and fibers. Most abundant tissue. Usually vascular, except cartilage. Includes bone, cartilage, adipose, tendons, ligaments and blood.

test.why: Cartilage has no blood vessels, unlike most connective tissues.

whyNot.0: Bone is a vascular connective tissue.
whyNot.1: Adipose tissue has a good blood supply.
whyNot.3: Areolar tissue is vascular and supplies the epithelium above it.

explain.body: Contractile and excitable. Skeletal is striated and voluntary; cardiac is striated, involuntary and found only in the heart; smooth is non-striated, involuntary and found in the walls of hollow organs.

test.q: Which muscle tissue is non-striated, involuntary and found in the walls of hollow organs?
test.why: Smooth muscle is non-striated and involuntary and sits in the walls of hollow organs, vessels and airways.

whyNot.1: Cardiac muscle is involuntary but striated, and it is found only in the heart.
whyNot.2: Skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary.
whyNot.3: The myocardium is the heart's cardiac muscle layer, which is striated.

explain.body: Neurons conduct electrical impulses. Neuroglia (glial cells) support, nourish and protect the neurons but do not conduct impulses themselves.

test.q: Which cells in nervous tissue support and protect neurons rather than conduct impulses?
test.why: Neuroglia (glial cells) are the support cells of nervous tissue.

whyNot.1: Interneurons are neurons that link other neurons; they conduct impulses.
whyNot.2: Motor neurons conduct impulses out to muscles and glands.
whyNot.3: Sensory neurons conduct impulses in from receptors.
